national_partners.notes: Cyber agency searched: Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC), within ASD, 2026-10-19 (en); found. In that check the live pages of the department and of the ACSC could not be retrieved, so the department's institute page, ASD's about page and the ACSC's about page were read in archived copies of 15 October, 15 September and 26 September 2026. Cooperation is stated with ASD (the host of ACSC), not with ACSC by name. On 10 November 2026 the government said it would propose a new targeted regulator for AI safety that would work with the institute to provide technical expertise and oversight; the regulator is not yet named or established, so it is not an entry. The National Cyber Security Coordinator is a role supported by the National Office of Cyber Security.

testing_capacity.notes: The minister's speech, marked check against delivery, says the institute is already testing frontier AI models 'with technical partners'; this does not make a partner the tester, so testing by other bodies is not recorded. No published evaluation was found. On 18 September 2026 the institute's General Manager said at a parliamentary committee hearing (uncorrected proof Hansard) 'I don't have a number to hand of exactly how many models we've tested' and referred to 'some of our early testing' on the capabilities of a newly released model, Astra. Joint network testing before the institute existed is credited to Australia, not the institute: testing reported, 2025-06-26 (multilingual exercise: 'Australia and Japan also ran independent tests in Mandarin Chinese and Japanese') and 2025-07-17 (agentic exercise: 'UK AISI, EU AI Office and Australia ran evaluations on two open-source models').

model_access.notes: No access event is recorded: the sources do not establish access to a named model before its public release or beyond publicly available access. The MOU is 'a statement of intent and is not intended to have legal effect' and contains no access term; Anthropic's announcement commits it to joint safety and security evaluations with the institute. On 6 October 2026 Anthropic said it was 'finalizing an agreement with the AI Safety Institute to enable it to run its own independent evaluations of our models'; no report of its conclusion was found. On 18 September 2026 a deputy secretary of the department told a parliamentary committee that colleagues in the National Intelligence Community were working with the companies and the US government 'to make sure we secure the access that we need to do the testing and evaluation that we need'. No legal power: Australia has no AI act. At a Senate estimates hearing on 29 October 2026 (uncorrected proof Hansard) a deputy secretary said the institute was still working through the technical aspects of how Anthropic and Microsoft, with which it has MOUs, would give it access to frontier models. The General Manager said that in the meantime the institute reaches Anthropic models through its technical partners, and that it tested frontier models with those partners in June 2026; she took on notice which models, so no event is recorded.

excerpts.text: Kate Conroy

a top priority has been getting the AI Safety Institute (AISI) up and running with the right people to lead it. Because we are not building a think tank. We are building a national testing capability.
In Dr Kate Conroy, the Government has that person, and she is supported by a great team.
Australia has established the AI Safety Institute.

The first is analysing and testing new AI models and applications. Here, as elsewhere, AISI has hit the ground running. It's already testing frontier AI models with technical partners. Not in year three. Not after a review. In its first month of operations.

This month, Professor Paul Salmon, a leading international expert, will start as AISI's Safety Science Research Lead. The broader AISI team also includes experts who have worked at the UK AI Security Institute and Google DeepMind.

One of AISI's key roles is to be a central expert capability that identifies those risks and builds a shared understanding of them across government so that policymakers and regulators can act with insight and evidence. This combines ongoing systems testing with active monitoring of risks and harms.

excerpts.text: The National AI Centre (NAIC) is the Australian Government’s lead body helping organisations understand and use AI safely.
NAIC develops and shares clear guidance, tools, templates, practical examples, programs and trusted information

sources.title: National Cyber Security Coordinator

excerpts.text: The National Cyber Security Coordinator (the Coordinator), supported by the National Office of Cyber Security, drives forward the necessary work to ensure Australia is best positioned to respond to the opportunities and threats of the digital age.
and triages action in response to a significant cyber incident

sources.title: Office of AI

excerpts.text: The Office of AI was established in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet on 15 July 2026.
The office will coordinate across Australian Government agencies to design and legislate the new Australia artificial intelligence (AI) standard

sources.title: About us

excerpts.text: To support the Prime Minister, the Cabinet and our portfolio ministers to improve the lives of all Australians, advance Australia’s interests, and keep our country safe and prosperous.

sources.title: Who we are

excerpts.text: We are Services Australia, an Australian Government agency within the Finance portfolio. We support Australians by efficiently delivering high-quality, accessible services and payments on behalf of the government.
